name: lemon
desc: LALR(1) parser generator like yacc or bison
why: A compact LALR parser generator from SQLite's author with an unusual grammar-as-config design, a door into how parsers are built.

brief.what_it_is: Lemon is an LALR(1) parser generator, a C-oriented tool in the same family as yacc and bison. You give it a context-free grammar and it converts that grammar into a subroutine that parses input using the grammar. The homepage describes it as a two-file source distribution: lemon.c is the generator program, and lempar.c is the template for the generated parser. The page does not describe the exact input file format or the output file names.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Lemon as a yacc/bison alternative with a grammar syntax that is less prone to programming errors, a re-entrant and thread-safe generated parser, and a non-terminal destructor mechanism intended to make leak-free parsers easier to write. It is maintained as part of the SQLite project and is used there as the parser for SQLite.
brief.how_it_works: The page gives only a high-level account. Lemon reads a grammar and generates a parser subroutine by filling in the lempar.c template. Non-terminal destructors are a feature for releasing memory attached to symbols when the parser discards them. The page does not explain the grammar file syntax or the generated API.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no install steps. The complete source is two files, lemon.c and lempar.c, and both are public domain. The homepage does not mention a compiler, build commands, or runtime requirements. Homebrew's formula is named lemon and installs an executable called lemon. No accounts or configuration are mentioned.
brief.standout: Lemon is smaller than bison and yacc, and its generated parser is re-entrant and thread-safe by design. Non-terminal destructors are built into the design, which targets one of the most common error sources in hand-written parser actions, memory leaks on error paths. Its author is the SQLite author, and SQLite itself is the main real-world example.
brief.status: Maintained, per the homepage, which says "Lemon is maintained as part of the SQLite project." The page shows no release version or date and no commit history, so I could not confirm recent activity beyond that statement.
brief.caveats: Lemon is not compatible with yacc or bison grammars, so existing grammars cannot be reused without rewriting. The homepage contains no example grammar, no command lines, and no usage instructions, and it points to documentation I did not fetch. The 'grammar as config' framing in the scout notes is not in the homepage text, which emphasizes syntax safety rather than configuration. The homepage links to SQLite's source as the example, but the captured text did not include those URLs.
quotes: The Lemon program is an LALR(1) parser generator.
Lemon using a different grammar syntax which is less prone to programming errors.
The parser generated by Lemon is both re-entrant and thread-safe.
Both the source code to lemon itself and the code that lemon generates are in the public domain.
